t:
Section 1005(e)(3) of the Detainee Treatment Act of 2005 (title X of Public Law 109–148; 119 Stat. 2740; 10 U.S.C. 801 note) is amended—
    (1) in subparagraph (A), by striking “pursuant to Military Commission Order No. 1. dated August 31, 2005 (or any successor military order)” and inserting “by a military commission under chapter 47A of title 10, United States Code”;  
    (2) by striking subparagraph (B) and inserting the following new subparagraph (B): 
“(B) Grant of review.—Review under this paragraph shall be as of right.”;  
    (3) in subparagraph (C)—
        (A) in clause (i)—
            (i) by striking “pursuant to the military order” and inserting “by a military commission”; and  
            (ii) by striking “at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba”; and   
        (B) in clause (ii), by striking “pursuant to such military order” and inserting “by the military commission”; and   
    (4) in subparagraph (D)(i), by striking “specified in the military order” and inserting “specified for a military commission”.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that making review "as of right" grants an outside party a right to sue over a federal decision. But this section only makes technical amendments to existing appellate review of military commission judgments against individual detainees, which is an appeal from an adjudication rather than outside involvement in a federal policy decision. It creates no comment period, hearing, advisory body, or consultation with outside parties, and mostly describes the scope of court review.
fable.s: “(B) Grant of review.—Review under this paragraph shall be as of right.”

opus.w: These amendments change the scope and mechanics of judicial review of military commission convictions under the Detainee Treatment Act, mostly by replacing references to the old military order. Making review 'as of right' gives a convicted defendant an appeal of an adjudication against him. That is like the manufacturer's defensive response in Example 11, not outside participation in a federal policy decision. Defining a court's jurisdiction over appeals falls within the listed trap for jurisdiction and litigation mechanics, so 'review' does not make this participation.
opus.s: “(B) Grant of review.—Review under this paragraph shall be as of right.”;
opus.b:
1. **The tempting reading:** The new subparagraph (B) says "Review under this paragraph shall be as of right." That could look like giving an outside party (a detainee) the right to challenge a federal decision in court, which would count as participation.

2. **Why it fails:** This provision amends the D.C. Circuit's jurisdiction to review final military commission decisions. It changes that review from discretionary to automatic and updates references from the old military order to the statutory commissions. The "decision" here is a criminal conviction of the individual, so this is a defendant's appeal, not outside input into a federal policy decision. That matches the defensive response in Example 11 and the listed trap about court jurisdiction and review mechanics. The other amendments are technical wording changes. I'm only moderately confident, because a literal reading of "right to sue a decision" could reach the other way.

qwen_chat.w: This section amends the Detainee Treatment Act to clarify that review by military commissions is a matter of right. While this grants a legal right to review, it is a procedural provision regarding judicial/military commission jurisdiction rather than a requirement for the federal government to consult with outside parties, hold public hearings, or form advisory committees before making a decision. The definition excludes litigation mechanics and focuses on pre-decision consultation or coordination with non-federal entities. This text merely updates statutory references and confirms a right to appeal/review, which falls under the litigation exception.
qwen_chat.s: (2) by striking subparagraph (B) and inserting the following new subparagraph (B): “(B) Grant of review.—Review under this paragraph shall be as of right.”;
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that granting a detainee the "right to review" constitutes participation because it allows an outside party to challenge a government decision. However, the definition explicitly excludes "a court's jurisdiction, venue, or the statute-of-limitations period for suits" and distinguishes between granting a right to sue/object and the procedural mechanics of litigation. More importantly, this section is purely technical, amending statutory references to align with the Military Commissions Act. It does not establish a new participatory process, advisory body, or consultation requirement; it merely clarifies the legal basis for existing judicial review. The "participation" here is judicial review, which is generally treated as litigation rather than the administrative participation defined (consultation, advisory boards, public comments). Furthermore, the text itself contains no language requiring consultation with outsiders, public hearings, or advisory committees.
